topic.name: EGFR-mutant lung cancer: resistance to osimertinib
topic.question: New evidence on how EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer becomes resistant to osimertinib, how often each mechanism occurs, and what works after resistance.

Treatment line or setting, e.g. first-line osimertinib, after progression.

Number of patients, if stated. Digits only.
What kind of finding the paper reports. Exactly one of the allowed values.

paper.title: EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma with leptomeningeal metastasis after osimertinib treatment: intrathecal chemotherapy combined with targeted therapy supported by cerebrospinal fluid next generation sequencing - a case report.
paper.abstract: Background: Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) is a severe complication of advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Conventional cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytology has limited sensitivity and often delays diagnosis. We report a case of LM molecularly supported by CSF next-generation sequencing (NGS) after three negative cytological examinations. NGS also revealed a potential bypass resistance alteration that informed subsequent treatment considerations. Case: A 57-year-old female never-smoker had EGFR exon 21 p.L858R-mutant lung adenocarcinoma. After 18 months of first-line osimertinib (80 mg once daily), she developed progressive nausea, vomiting, and dizziness. Contrast-enhanced cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed linear leptomeningeal enhancement. Lumbar puncture showed markedly elevated intracranial pressure (>300 mmH2O) and increased CSF protein. However, three CSF cytological examinations (including cell block sections) found no malignant cells. CSF NGS detected the EGFR p.L858R mutation identical to the primary tumor, together with CDK4 amplification. Integrated with the clinical and MRI presentation, these findings supported a diagnosis of probable LM and suggested cell-cycle bypass activation as a potential mechanism associated with osimertinib resistance. After intrathecal methotrexate plus continued oral osimertinib, her neurological symptoms improved markedly, and intracranial pressure returned to normal. The first seizure occurred on March 19, 2026, and MRI on April 8, 2026 confirmed new brain parenchymal metastases. Whole-brain radiotherapy with a local boost to the metastases, antiepileptic treatment, and continued osimertinib led to obvious shrinkage of the intracranial lesions. Grade 3 thrombocytopenia and severe malnutrition occurred during multimodal therapy and improved with supportive care. At the last follow-up, the patient was clinically stable with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG PS) of 1. Conclusions: CSF NGS can overcome the diagnostic bottleneck of cytology-negative LM. It can also identify potential resistance alterations and actionable targets (such as CDK4/6 inhibitors) at the same time, providing direction for subsequent targeted strategies. As part of multimodal therapy, intrathecal chemotherapy combined with an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) can contribute to disease control in the CSF compartment, whereas parenchymal progression still requires salvage radiotherapy. Cumulative hematological and nutritional toxicity should be monitored during sequential multimodal therapy.

paper.title: [Resistance Mechanisms and Recent Advances in the Third-generation EGFR-TKI Osimertinib for Non-small Cell Lung Cancer].
paper.abstract: Lung cancer is one of the malignant tumors with the highest morbidity and mortality worldwide, and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for approximately 85% of all lung cancer cases, with lung adenocarcinoma being the predominant histological subtype. Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) sensitizing mutations are among the most common and important actionable driver alterations in Chinese patients with lung adenocarcinoma, and the advent of EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) has inaugurated a new era of precision targeted therapy for lung adenocarcinoma. Osimertinib, a third-generation EGFR-TKI, has become the standard first-line treatment for advanced EGFR-mutated NSCLC and substantially improves survival; however, acquired resistance remains the central limitation to long-term benefit. This review first delineates the distinction between primary and acquired resistance, then summarizes the principal mechanisms underlying acquired resistance to Osimertinib, including EGFR-dependent alterations, bypass pathway activation, histological transformation and cellular plasticity, tumour microenvironment remodelling and metabolic reprogramming, as well as recently identified mechanisms such as SWI/SNF-related, matrix-associated, actin-dependent regulator of chromatin, subfamily A, member 4 (SMARCA4) loss, the YAP1/AXL axis and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) epigenetic adaptation. Based on the frequent co-occurrence of multiple resistance mechanisms, we further summarize clinical-scenario-based therapeutic strategies and representative domestic and international studies after resistance to third-generation EGFR-TKIs, so as to provide theoretical references for overcoming Osimertinib resistance. Overall, precise resistance profiling via rebiopsy and liquid biopsy, rational pathway-directed combination therapy, and the integration of next-generation EGFR inhibitors, antibody-drug conjugates and patient-derived organoid drug sensitivity testing are expected to transform EGFR-mutated NSCLC from inevitable resistance into a manageable chronic disease. .

paper.title: [Retrospective Analysis of the Efficacy and Safety of Amivantamab-containing Regimens in Patients with EGFR-mutant Lung Cancer and Leptomeningeal Metastases].
paper.abstract: Background: Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) is a devastating complication of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), occurring most frequently in patients with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant NSCLC. However, treatment options remain limited for patients who develop LM after treatment with the third-generation EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). This study evaluated the efficacy and safety of Amivantamab-containing regimens in this patient population. Methods: A total of 11 patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC and LM who received Amivantamab-containing regimens at Peking Union Medical College Hospital between February 2025 and July 2026 were retrospectively included. Neurological symptoms, findings on contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytology, LM-progression-free survival (PFS), and adverse events were evaluated. Follow-up for all patients was censored on July 31, 2026, with a median follow-up duration of 3.7 months (IQR: 2.1-7.0). Three patients had not yet reached the prespecified time point for their first standardized radiographic assessment by the data cutoff and were therefore censored in the follow-up analysis. Results: Among the 11 patients, 8 (72.7%) received Amivantamab in combination with a third-generation EGFR-TKI, whereas the remaining 3 patients received Amivantamab plus Pemetrexed, Amivantamab plus Zipalertinib, and Amivantamab monotherapy, respectively. Following treatment initiation, LM-related neurological symptoms improved in 8 patients (72.7%), with a time to symptom relief ranging from 1 to 7 days (median, 2.5 days). Among the 8 patients with evaluable post-baseline MRI, the best overall responses were complete response in 1 patient, partial response in 5 patients, and stable disease in 2 patients. Only three patients underwent post-treatment CSF cytologic reassessment; cytology clearance occurred in 2 patients and remained positive in 1 patient. During follow-up, 3 patients experienced disease progression, and 1 patient died before the first scheduled radiographic assessment. LM-PFS among the aforementioned 4 patients ranged from 1.7 to 9.7 months. Treatment-related adverse events were predominantly dermatologic/mucosal toxicities and infusion-related reactions. Two patients discontinued Amivantamab because of persistent dermatologic/mucosal toxicities and personal preference; one of these patients was rechallenged with Amivantamab after disease recurrence. No treatment-related deaths occurred. Conclusions: Amivantamab-containing multimodal treatment regimens were associated with symptom improvement and preliminary radiographic disease-control signals. However, because concomitant systemic therapies, intrathecal treatment, and CSF diversion procedures were present, the observed changes cannot be disentangled from or fully attributed to the independent effect of Amivantamab. The clinical benefit of Amivantamab in LM requires further validation in prospective studies.

paper.title: Structural Optimization of Pyrimidine-Based EGFR Inhibitors Against Resistance Mutations in NSCLC.
paper.abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a major global health burden, particularly among non-smoking Asian populations, in whom activating EGFR mutations are the predominant oncogenic drivers. The emergence of multiple resistance mutations like the T790M, C797S, and especially the clinically intractable L858R/T790M/C797S triple mutant, has rendered all existing tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) ineffective. Despite substantial advances across three generations of EGFR-TKIs, the therapeutic options available for resistant mutations remain limited. Currently no approved agent is capable of selectively and effectively targeting the triple mutant EGFR. This unmet clinical need highlights the urgency for continued drug discovery efforts aimed at overcoming resistance mediated by the C797S mutation. This need has driven intensive efforts toward developing inhibitors capable of overcoming C797S-mediated resistance. Among the scaffolds explored, pyrimidine has emerged as particularly tractable, offering favorable ligand efficiency, synthetic accessibility and multiple substitution vectors that project into the T790M-remodeled hydrophobic pocket and the region vacated by Cys797, while engaging the conserved Met793 of the hinge region. This review presents, an overview of the key structural features of the EGFR's ATP-binding site is provided to facilitate a deeper understanding of the rational design of future EGFR inhibitors.

paper.title: Osimertinib resistance in non-small cell lung cancer is mediated by sustained AKT activation through lipid raft-dependent insulin signaling.
paper.abstract: Acquired resistance to osimertinib remains a major challenge in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Using an osimertinib-resistant (AR) cell model lacking the on-target EGFR C797S mutation, we uncover sustained AKT phosphorylation under osimertinib treatment driven by insulin receptor (INSR) signaling. Notably, INSR-AKT activation is observed exclusively in AR cells, whereas parental H1975 cells fail to activate AKT even following INSR overexpression or exogenous insulin stimulation. Cholesterol depletion abolishes the INSR-AKT response in AR cells, indicating a lipid raft-dependent mechanism. Consistently, INSR localizes within lipid rafts in AR but not in parental H1975 cells. Proteomic profiling reveals the enrichment of lipid raft-associated proteins in AR cells. Among them, flotillin-1 (FLOT1) is identified as a key raft scaffold mediating INSR-AKT signaling and osimertinib resistance through functional shRNA screening. Co-immunoprecipitation and proximity ligation assay confirm a cholesterol-dependent interaction between FLOT1 and INSR. Functionally, FLOT1 knockdown disrupts raft-associated INSR localization, attenuates AKT activation, and reduces the IC50 of osimertinib in AR cells. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that lipid raft-dependent INSR-AKT signaling contributes to osimertinib resistance in NSCLC.

paper.title: Mechanism-Matched Pharmacology of Resistance in EGFR-Mutant NSCLC: Genomic Bypass, Lineage Plasticity, Antibody-Drug Conjugates, and Candidate Biophysical Targets.
paper.abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) often responds to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors but develops heterogeneous resistance. This structured narrative review integrates clinical and experimental evidence on resistance after osimertinib and intensified EGFR-directed therapy. It distinguishes on-target EGFR alterations, MET and ERBB-family bypass, downstream signaling, oncogenic fusions, histologic transformation, epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity, and drug-tolerant persistence, linking each mechanism to an appropriate assay and treatment context. We evaluate next-generation EGFR inhibitors, EGFR-MET combinations, bispecific antibodies, platinum-pemetrexed intensification, and antibody-drug conjugates directed at HER3, TROP2, or HER2. Clinical validation is assessed separately from mechanistic causality, with attention to allelic phase, central nervous system exposure, target engagement, unbound drug concentration, predictive biomarkers, and safety. Ion channels and transporters, including ANO1/TMEM16A, LRRC8/VRAC, KCa3.1, hERG, STIM-ORAI, TRP, and pH regulators, remain exploratory candidate targets. Available evidence for their role in acquired osimertinib resistance is largely indirect; expression or general tumor biology does not establish disease-specific dependency. A mechanism-matched development pathway using paired tissue and plasma sampling, relevant resistant models, causal perturbation, and pharmacodynamic validation is proposed. Clinical decisions should follow validated mechanisms rather than extrapolated biophysical hypotheses.

paper.title: Management of Advanced EGFR-Mutant Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer Across the Disease Course.
paper.abstract: Advances in targeted therapy have improved outcomes for patients with advanced epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors and first-line combination regimens have expanded treatment options, making the balance between survival benefit, toxicity, treatment burden, and individual patient fitness increasingly important in initial treatment selection. As acquired resistance continues to limit the duration of benefit, this decision must also be considered in the context of subsequent care. At progression, tissue and plasma profiling provide complementary information that can help characterize the diverse mechanisms of resistance and guide further treatment. As resistance-directed therapies and antibody-drug conjugates expand the available treatment options, their selection requires consideration of prior therapy and the pattern of progression, together with molecular findings where relevant. This review examines these interconnected decisions across the course of advanced EGFR-mutant NSCLC, from first-line treatment selection to the assessment and management of acquired resistance. We also address central nervous system involvement, uncommon EGFR mutations, and exon 20 insertions as distinct clinical settings in which disease distribution and the underlying molecular alteration shape treatment choices. By integrating clinical and translational evidence, we discuss how these factors may inform treatment sequencing and individualized care, with attention to survival, quality of life, and the cumulative burden of therapy across the disease course.
